newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Gore urges Latin Americans to clean environment.
newsitem.headline: Gore urges Latin Americans to clean environment.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Saturday told Latin Americans to stop looking to their governments to clean up rivers, lands and skies, saying citizens and companies should help preserve the environment.
"Governments alone cannot provide all the solutions," he told a one-day regional summit on sustainable economic development in this eastern Bolivian city.
"The private sector, non-governmental organisations and international financial institutions have increasingly important roles to play."
Sustainable development, a principle approved by world leaders at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, means pursuing economic growth without harming the environment.

At the end of the day-long summit, envoys from 27 nations, including 14 heads of state, approved a 65-point declaration calling for better legislation to protect the environment, more popular participation in nature preservation projects and the search for new ways of financing.
Chile's President Eduardo Frei announced the next Summit of the Americas to be held in his country will take place on March 28-29, 1998.

The first was hosted by U.S. President Bill Clinton in December 1994 in Miami and was attended by 34 heads of state from throughout the Americas. Cuba's Communist leader Fidel Castro was the only regional head of state who was not invited.
Gore told reporters the meeting was a great success and would generate concrete steps to preserve the environment.
"I think you are going to see specific results out of this conference. We have teams in place that are continuing the dialogue and working groups that are already making a lot of progress," he said.

His plane was diverted to Cochabamba, 150 miles (250 km) west of Santa Cruz due to heavy rains in this tropical city. The vice president arrived four hours behind schedule in Santa Cruz, causing the summit to open 90 minutes late.

In his speech, Gore, who has had a longstanding interest in environmental issues, called for urgent, concerted action so that all Latin Americans, 40 percent of whom live under the poverty line, have access to clean water and electricity.

The meeting's host, Bolivia's President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, proposed that North, Central and South American nations draft agreements on sustainable development for 2005, when they hope to set up a pan-American free trade zone.
"The real possibility to achieve sustainable development is ... here, provided we are ready to work without trepidation on an all- encompassing treaty," the Bolivian leader said.

But despite the optimistic tone of the speeches, both organisational problems and differences over the agenda hunted the conference, leading several leaders to cancel their visit and others to cut it short, often using only bland excuses.
Only 14 heads of state showed up for the gathering, which was cut down to one day from the original two. Bolivia had announced last Monday that 24 leaders would attend.

Officials have said off-the-record that the main problem was a lack of consensus on the scope of the meeting, with Washington insisting on focusing on the environment and several Latin American nations arguing that poverty and economic development should take precedence.
"Many (heads of state) did not show up because they did not know what they would be discussing," an official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Gore called that view "a total misrepresentation", saying it was normal for heads of state to be unable to attend international meetings and send other officials instead.

In a separate, four-day forum that ended Friday in La Paz, 300 miles (500 km) west of Santa Cruz, first ladies from the Americas, including U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, demanded equal access to high public positions for women.
